A pH near 9 suits the pancreatic proteases in the duodenum. Matching an enzyme's optimum to a region of the tract is the whole point of the experiment.

cards.q: What is the approximate optimal pH for trypsin and pancreatic amylase?
cards.a: About 8.
options: About 8
About 11
About 2
About 4
cards.explanation: Pancreatic enzymes work in the duodenum after bicarbonate has neutralized chyme, so their optimum sits in the mildly alkaline range near pH 8. A pH near 2 is gastric and would denature them. A pH near 4 is too acidic for full activity, which is why insufficient bicarbonate impairs digestion. A pH near 11 is far outside anything the body produces and would denature the enzyme.

cards.q: In a starch digestion experiment, what does a drop of iodine solution detect?
cards.a: Starch, by turning blue black.
options: Reducing sugars, by turning orange
Starch, by turning blue black
Protein, by turning purple
Fat, by turning the solution cloudy
cards.explanation: Iodine forms a blue black complex with the helical structure of starch, so a tube that stays dark still contains starch and a tube that turns pale has had its starch digested. Reducing sugars are detected by Benedict solution, which turns orange or red. Protein is detected by the biuret test, which turns purple. Fat is not detected by iodine.

cards.q: In a digestive enzyme experiment, what is the purpose of a tube containing substrate but no enzyme?
cards.a: It is a negative control showing the substrate does not change alone.
options: It measures the optimal temperature for the reaction in that tube
It provides the baseline pH against which the other tubes are read
It is a positive control that shows the test can detect the product
It is a negative control showing the substrate does not change alone
cards.explanation: A tube with substrate and no enzyme tells you whether any change you see in the other tubes needed the enzyme, which is the only way to attribute the result to enzyme activity. A positive control would be a tube known to produce the product. Temperature is set by a water bath, not by a tube composition. pH is set deliberately in each tube by buffer.

cards.q: At what temperature do human digestive enzymes work best in a laboratory assay?
cards.a: About 37 C.
options: About 60 C
About 4 C
About 25 C
About 37 C
cards.explanation: Enzyme optima match the environment the enzyme evolved in, and for a human enzyme that is core body temperature near 37 C. At 4 C molecular motion is too slow and the reaction nearly stops, though the enzyme is undamaged. Room temperature at 25 C gives a slow but measurable reaction. By 60 C most human enzymes are denaturing rather than accelerating.

cards.q: What happens to an enzyme that has been boiled for five minutes and then cooled back to 37 C?
cards.a: It stays inactive, because denaturation of its shape is not reversible.
options: It works only at the higher temperature and stops when cooled
It regains full activity once the temperature is back in range
It stays inactive, because denaturation of its shape is not reversible
It becomes twice as active, because heat breaks it into more active fragments
cards.explanation: Boiling disrupts the hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions that hold the active site in shape, and for most enzymes that unfolding cannot be undone by cooling. This is the key distinction from cold inhibition, where activity returns on warming. Heat does not fragment an enzyme into more active pieces. An enzyme that had been destroyed does not work at any temperature.

cards.q: An enzyme acts on starch but produces no change when incubated with a protein solution. What property does this demonstrate?
cards.a: Substrate specificity.
options: Denaturation
Substrate specificity
Temperature dependence
Competitive inhibition
cards.explanation: An active site has a shape and chemistry that fit one substrate or one class of bond, so amylase cleaves alpha 1,4 glycosidic bonds and simply cannot bind a polypeptide. Temperature dependence would be shown by varying heat, not substrate. Competitive inhibition requires a molecule that binds the active site and blocks it. Denaturation would abolish activity on all substrates, including starch.

cards.q: In an experiment testing amylase at pH 2, 7, and 9 at 37 C, what is the independent variable?
cards.a: pH.
options: pH
The amount of starch digested
The concentration of amylase
Temperature
cards.explanation: The independent variable is the one the experimenter deliberately changes across tubes, which here is pH, while temperature and enzyme concentration are held constant as controlled variables. The amount of starch digested is what you measure, making it the dependent variable. Naming these correctly is what lets you attribute a difference between tubes to the factor you varied.

cards.q: Amylase and starch are incubated together at pH 2 and 37 C for 30 minutes, then tested with iodine. Predict the result.
cards.a: The tube stays blue black, because amylase is inactive at pH 2.
options: The tube turns orange, because acid hydrolyzes the starch itself
The tube turns pale, because amylase works at any pH given enough time
The tube stays blue black, because amylase is inactive at pH 2
The tube turns purple, because iodine detects the maltose produced
cards.explanation: Amylase works near neutral pH and is inactive in strong acid, so the starch remains and iodine still finds it. Time cannot compensate for a pH that has denatured or inhibited the enzyme. Iodine detects starch, not maltose, and it never turns purple. Dilute acid at 37 C for half an hour does not appreciably hydrolyze starch on its own.

cards.q: Pepsin and egg white protein are incubated at pH 8 and 37 C. Predict the result and explain it.
cards.a: Little or no digestion occurs, because pepsin requires an acidic environment.
options: Digestion occurs but the products are reassembled at alkaline pH
Rapid digestion occurs, because 37 C is optimal for all human enzymes
Little or no digestion occurs, because pepsin requires an acidic environment
Rapid digestion occurs, because pH 8 matches the optimum for all proteases
cards.explanation: Pepsin is an acid protease and is essentially inert at pH 8, which is exactly the mechanism that ends its action when chyme reaches the duodenum. Optimal temperature cannot rescue an enzyme that is outside its pH range. Not all proteases share an optimum, since trypsin prefers alkaline conditions and pepsin does not. Hydrolysis is not reversed by raising pH.

cards.q: Two tubes contain amylase and starch. One is boiled before incubation and one is not. After 30 minutes at 37 C, what difference does iodine reveal?
cards.a: The boiled tube stays blue black and the unboiled tube turns pale.
options: The boiled tube turns pale and the unboiled tube stays blue black
Both tubes turn pale, because boiling only slows the enzyme temporarily
Both tubes stay blue black, because iodine inhibits amylase
The boiled tube stays blue black and the unboiled tube turns pale
cards.explanation: Boiling denatures amylase permanently, so the starch survives and the iodine test stays positive, while the untreated enzyme digests the starch and the color fades. Iodine is added after incubation as a detector and does not inhibit the enzyme during the reaction. Reversing the two results would imply that heat activates the enzyme. Boiling is not a temporary slowdown; that describes chilling.

cards.q: An enzyme tube is kept in an ice bath instead of a 37 C water bath, and almost no product forms. It is then warmed to 37 C and product appears. What does this show?
cards.a: Cold slows the reaction without denaturing, so the effect is reversible.
options: Cold denatures the enzyme in exactly the same way that heat does
Cold slows the reaction without denaturing, so the effect is reversible
Cold changes the pH of the buffer, and warming it back restores it
Cold destroys the substrate, and warming allows new substrate to form
cards.explanation: At low temperature molecules collide less often and with less energy, so the reaction rate falls, but the enzyme's folded structure is intact and full activity returns on warming. Heat denaturation is different precisely because it is not reversible, which is why this pair of experiments is worth doing. Buffer pH shifts only slightly with temperature and would not explain the result. Substrate is not destroyed by cold and cannot regenerate.

cards.q: Lipase, cream, and a pH indicator are incubated at 37 C. What change in the indicator do you predict, and why?
cards.a: The indicator shifts toward acidic, because free fatty acids are released.
options: The indicator does not change, because lipase does not alter pH
The indicator shifts toward alkaline, because bicarbonate is produced instead
The indicator shifts toward acidic, because free fatty acids are released
The indicator shifts toward alkaline, because glycerol is a base
cards.explanation: Lipase cleaves triglyceride into a monoglyceride and two fatty acids, and those free carboxyl groups release H+, so the pH of the tube falls measurably over the incubation. Glycerol is a neutral alcohol and is not even a major product of pancreatic lipase. Something must change or the assay would not work. Nothing in the reaction generates bicarbonate.

cards.q: A tube containing pancreatic amylase and gelatin, a protein, shows no product after incubation at pH 8 and 37 C. What is the best conclusion?
cards.a: Amylase is specific for carbohydrate and cannot act on protein.
options: The enzyme was denatured by the gelatin in the tube
The incubation was far too short for any enzyme to act
The pH of 8 was wrong for amylase, so no reaction could occur
Amylase is specific for carbohydrate and cannot act on protein
cards.explanation: The conditions were correct for pancreatic amylase, so the absence of product points to the substrate rather than the environment, demonstrating that active sites are selective. A pH of 8 is close to this enzyme's optimum, so the pH explanation fails. Substrates do not denature enzymes. Blaming the incubation time would require a control showing that amylase also failed on starch, which is not the case.

cards.q: Adding bile salts to a tube of lipase and cream increases the rate at which pH falls. Does this make bile an enzyme?
cards.a: No, because bile salts only increase the surface area available to lipase.
options: Yes, because bile salts speed up a chemical reaction
No, because bile salts only increase the surface area available to lipase
Yes, because bile salts are consumed during the reaction
No, because bile salts lower the pH themselves rather than aiding digestion
cards.explanation: An enzyme catalyzes bond breaking, and bile salts break no bonds; they disperse the fat so more of it is exposed to the enzyme already present. That is a physical effect on substrate availability, not catalysis. Bile salts are not consumed, and if anything they are recovered intact. They do not acidify the tube; the fatty acids released by lipase do that.

cards.q: An unknown digestive enzyme shows high activity at pH 2, no activity at pH 7, and no activity at pH 9, and it digests protein but not starch. Identify the enzyme and the region it works in, and predict what happens to it when chyme reaches the duodenum.
cards.a: It is pepsin from the stomach, and it is inactivated as pancreatic bicarbonate raises the pH.
options: It is salivary amylase from the mouth, and it is inactivated by gastric acid
It is pancreatic lipase, and it is denatured by the acid it encounters in the stomach
It is trypsin from the pancreas, and it becomes more active as bicarbonate raises the pH there
It is pepsin from the stomach, and it is inactivated as pancreatic bicarbonate raises the pH
cards.explanation: Two pieces of data pin this down: an acid optimum places it in the stomach and a protein substrate makes it a protease, which together identify pepsin. Trypsin is a protease but has an alkaline optimum, so it would show the opposite pH profile. Amylase acts on starch, which this enzyme does not touch. Lipase acts on fat and prefers a near neutral pH.

cards.q: Two amylase tubes show no starch digestion. Tube A was boiled first, and tube B was buffered to pH 2. Design a single follow up step that tells the two apart and state the expected results.
cards.a: Neutralize both tubes to pH 7 and reincubate: tube B digests the starch and tube A does not.
options: Cool both tubes to 4 C and then reincubate: tube B digests the starch and tube A does not
Boil both tubes again and reincubate: tube A digests the starch and tube B does not
Neutralize both tubes to pH 7 and reincubate: tube B digests the starch and tube A does not
Add iodine to both tubes again: tube A turns pale and tube B stays dark
cards.explanation: Low pH inhibits reversibly in this range while boiling denatures permanently, so restoring a favorable pH separates a recoverable enzyme from a destroyed one. Boiling again would only destroy whatever activity remained in tube B. Repeating the iodine test adds no new information, since both tubes already tested positive for starch. Cooling would slow both reactions and reveal nothing about the difference.

cards.q: A data table shows enzyme X most active at pH 2 and enzyme Y most active at pH 8, and both act on protein. A third tube shows enzyme Y placed in a pH 2 buffer produces no product even after the pH is restored to 8. Interpret all three findings.
cards.a: X is a gastric protease and Y a pancreatic protease, and acid denatured Y for good.
options: X is a pancreatic protease and Y a gastric protease, and Y simply needs more time at pH 8
Both are gastric proteases, and the third tube shows that pH has no lasting effect at all
X and Y are the same enzyme measured twice, and the third tube shows a pipetting error
X is a gastric protease and Y a pancreatic protease, and acid denatured Y for good
cards.explanation: The pH optima assign each enzyme to the region whose pH matches it, and the failure to recover after acid exposure shows that extreme pH can denature as permanently as heat, which is why pepsin cannot be replaced by trypsin in the stomach. Two enzymes with opposite optima cannot be the same enzyme. Reversing the assignments contradicts the measured optima. If pH had no lasting effect, the third tube would have produced product once returned to pH 8.

cards.q: A student runs amylase with starch at pH 7 in three water baths: 4 C, 37 C, and 90 C. The 4 C and 90 C tubes both show undigested starch. Explain why the two negative results have different causes and predict what happens if each tube is moved to 37 C for another 30 minutes.
cards.a: The cold tube was only slowed and will digest the starch at 37 C, while the hot tube was denatured and will not.
options: Both were only slowed, so both will digest the starch at 37 C
The hot tube was only slowed and will digest the starch at 37 C, while the cold tube was denatured and will not
Both were denatured, so neither will digest the starch at 37 C
The cold tube was only slowed and will digest the starch at 37 C, while the hot tube was denatured and will not
cards.explanation: Identical results can have opposite mechanisms, which is exactly what makes the recovery test informative: low temperature reduces collision energy without unfolding the protein, while high temperature breaks the bonds that maintain the active site. Only the reversible case recovers on rewarming. Cold does not denature enzymes at these temperatures, so calling the cold tube the denatured one has the two causes exactly backward.
